b: Effective cost per mille (eCPM) is the revenue earned, or the money spent, for every 1,000 ad impressions, whatever the ad was actually sold on. "Mille" is Latin for thousand. The measure exists because advertising is priced in incompatible units: one campaign pays per thousand impressions, another per click, a third per install or sale. eCPM converts all of them into a single figure so a publisher can see which buyer paid most for the same space, and so ad servers and mediation tools can rank them against each other.

The formula is simple. Google's AdMob help centre states it as "(Total Earnings / Impressions) x 1000". A mobile app that earns $700 from 200,000 impressions has an eCPM of $3.50, according to AppsFlyer's glossary, which also notes the oddity in the name: "although eCPM includes the word 'cost', it actually measures revenue."
On the sell side, eCPM is a backward-looking average. It takes earnings already booked and divides them by impressions already served.

The value of the measure lies in normalisation. Consider a publisher choosing between two buyers for the same slot. Buyer A pays a $2.00 CPM. Buyer B pays $0.50 per click, and its ads are clicked 0.5 percent of the time. Per 1,000 impressions, buyer B generates five clicks, or $2.50. Its eCPM is $2.50, so it is the better buyer. The general conversion for click-priced demand is cost per click multiplied by click-through rate multiplied by 1,000. For install-priced demand, Unity's glossary gives eCPM as installs per 1,000 impressions (IPM) multiplied by cost per install (CPI).

That formula gives eCPM a buy-side role. Ad networks running cost-per-install campaigns rank advertisers on predicted eCPM, so a high bid with a weak creative can lose to a lower bid with a stronger install rate.
The phrase "eCPM" hides a choice of denominator, and different choices produce different numbers from the same revenue. Google Ad Manager's help page on Ad Exchange lists three:
Ad request eCPM divides revenue by all ad requests, including those that went unfilled.
Matched request eCPM divides revenue by requests that received an ad response.
Impressions eCPM divides revenue by impressions actually rendered. Google treats it as the default average eCPM.

"The further you go down the chain when you select a CPM denominator, the higher the CPM," the page states. A publisher with $1,200 in revenue from 1,000,000 requests and a 60 percent fill rate has an impressions eCPM of $2.00 but an ad request eCPM of only $1.20. That second figure is what PPC Land calls revenue per request, and it equals fill rate multiplied by impressions eCPM. Publishers who chase eCPM alone can raise it by turning away cheap demand while total revenue falls.
Where eCPM sits in the transaction flow

eCPM does its most visible work in mediation, which decides which ad network fills an app's slot. In the classic mediation waterfall, networks are called one at a time in order of their eCPM, highest first. If the first network declines, the request falls to the next.

Those values describe the past, not the impression at hand. AdMob's documentation distinguishes observed eCPM, "a third-party ad network's estimated average eCPM calculated using historical revenue data," from optimized average eCPM, the value used to place the network in the waterfall. AdMob updates the optimized value "twice a day using historical data," country by country. While it gathers data, a publisher can type in a manual eCPM to hold the network's position.

Waterfall lines also carry an eCPM floor, the minimum a network entry must pay. Publishers create several lines for one network, at $10, $5 and $2 for example, to approximate an auction without running one.

In-app bidding replaced much of that logic. Each network submits a real-time bid for the impression, and the highest wins. eCPM then becomes a reporting outcome rather than a ranking input, although floors remain. In July 2025, Google added InMobi, ironSource and Unity as bidders for all AdMob publishers and introduced bidding eCPM floors at mediation group level. Shimmer Games reported a 36 percent revenue increase and a 9 percent eCPM improvement after adjusting floors, a company case study.

On the web, Google Ad Manager uses a publisher-entered value CPM so that remnant line items sold through other networks can compete against real-time Ad Exchange bids. The price floor carried in an OpenRTB bid request's bidfloor field is a separate control, judged largely by its effect on eCPM.

eCPM emerged with the ad networks of the early web, when publishers needed to compare CPM display deals against pay-per-click text ads. By February 27, 2006, Theresa Chow of AdSense publisher support described eCPM on the Inside AdSense blog as "industry shorthand that seems here to stay," defining it as total earnings divided by impressions in thousands.

Web publishers built daisy chains of networks ranked by historical eCPM, which yield optimisers such as Admeld set out to automate. AdMob's purchase of AdWhirl in August 2009 brought the same logic to apps.

Google itself moved away from the term for AdSense. Its new interface, rolled out from late 2010, labelled the metric RPM, revenue per mille. Meredith Blackwell of the AdSense team wrote on February 18, 2011, that "RPM is just another term for eCPM, and it's calculated the same way." On November 8, 2011, Jamie Firkus wrote that the old interface said eCPM and the new one said RPM, and that "to avoid confusion in the future, we'll work to use only one term (RPM)." The formula Firkus gave was page-based: estimated earnings divided by page views, multiplied by 1,000.

AdMob kept eCPM as a reporting and waterfall concept. The arrival of in-app bidding, beginning with Facebook tests in 2017 and Google's open bidding beta in March 2018, gradually shifted eCPM from ranking input to outcome. Google Ads stopped buying multicall waterfall requests in October 2023, and DV360 stopped bidding on multiple waterfall calls to Google Ad Manager and the AdMob Network on October 23, 2024.

For publishers and app developers, eCPM is the first number in most revenue dashboards, and changes in it drive decisions on floors, ad placement and which networks to keep. Its movements are often read as signs of demand health. During a Google Ad Manager disruption in January 2026, publishers reported page RPM falls of between 63 and 90 percent across language versions of a single site, and one Reddit user said: "We've lost around 70% of our eCPM in the last three months with the same traffic and the same banner placements."
For advertisers, the conversion of click and action bids into implied eCPM explains why creative performance affects whether a campaign wins at all.

It ignores what went unsold. Impressions eCPM rises if cheap impressions are removed, even when revenue falls. Ezoic said in September 2026 that rendering ads only near the viewport cut display impressions by about 25 percent and lifted viewability to 87 percent; the company said revenue "held" rather than rose, a reminder that a higher price per thousand need not mean more money.
It is a lagging estimate. Waterfalls ranked by historical eCPM call networks in an order based on past averages. Bidding was built to fix that.
Reported values may differ from paid values. AdMob's glossary warns that for waterfall sources, eCPM "may not match the above formula due to invalid traffic."

Hybrid versus bidding-only performance is contested. MonetizeMore CEO Kean Graham wrote in November 2026 that hybrid setups, which combine bidding with eCPM-floored waterfall lines, typically beat bidding-only stacks by 10 to 20 percent, a figure he called MonetizeMore's average. Nathan Sadeh, who lists his role as senior analyst at AppLovin, replied in personal comments that AppLovin's data "doesn't show the uplift mentioned, especially not on gaming." Neither side published underlying data.
CPM is a price agreed in advance: the rate an advertiser pays per 1,000 impressions on a CPM-priced buy. eCPM is a calculated average that can apply to any pricing model.

RPM in Google's AdSense usage is page-based, dividing earnings by page views rather than impressions. A page with three ad units produces one page view but three impressions, so page RPM is usually higher than impressions eCPM. Ezoic's EPMV, earnings per thousand visitors, uses visits as the denominator, and revenue per session is a related measure.

Win CPM is the average price a buyer pays on auctions it wins. As PPC Land's explainer on win CPM puts it, eCPM "measures earnings, not a buyer's clearing price." The two differ by fees taken between buyer and seller.

The waterfall, where eCPM floors still decide outcomes, is under pressure. PPC Land reported on November 16, 2026, that AppLovin had quietly stopped publishers creating new waterfall lines for its network on rival mediation platforms, and that existing lines could no longer have their eCPM floor changed, according to GameBiz Consulting's Božo Janković. Six days later, Graham said the restriction also applied in Google Ad Manager, writing that "the floors are frozen, so no new price points." No AppLovin announcement was found.
The same day, Google said it would test Ask AdMob, a Gemini-based assistant that checks third-party configurations for floor price discrepancies.

Measurement changes will also move the denominator. From February 17, 2027, AdSense and Ad Manager will count display impressions only once rendering begins. Fewer counted impressions for the same revenue would, mechanically, push reported eCPM up.

Who: Publishers, app developers and their yield teams use eCPM to compare demand sources; ad networks and mediation platforms such as AdMob, AppLovin MAX, Unity LevelPlay and Google Ad Manager use it to rank and floor demand; advertisers meet it when click or install bids are converted for auctions.

What: eCPM, effective cost per mille, is revenue or spend per 1,000 impressions, calculated as earnings divided by impressions multiplied by 1,000, regardless of the pricing model used. Different denominators, such as requests or matched requests, give different values.

When: The term was in common use by 2006. Google replaced it with RPM in AdSense between 2010 and 2011, while AdMob kept it. In-app bidding from 2017 onward moved it from ranking input to reporting outcome.

Where: It appears in publisher revenue reports, in mediation waterfalls as historical and optimized values, in eCPM floors on waterfall lines and bidding groups, and in ad network auctions that convert CPC and CPI bids.
Why: Advertising is sold in incompatible units. eCPM puts them on a common scale, though it ignores unsold inventory, relies on historical estimates and can rise while total revenue falls.
